story: A federal jury in Brooklyn convicted Chinese company Huawei on 10 of 12 counts including conspiracy to steal trade secrets, bank fraud and sanctions violations related to Iran, while acquitting it of racketeering.
title: Huawei guilty of fraud and trade secret conspiracy, not racketeering
dek: A Brooklyn jury found Huawei guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including sanctions violations and trade-secret theft, but not racketeering.
body:
A federal jury in Brooklyn on Tuesday convicted Chinese telecom company Huawei on 10 of 12 criminal counts. Guilty counts include bank fraud, wire fraud, money laundering, sanctions violations tied to Iran, and conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Jurors acquitted Huawei of racketeering, the charge that would have called it a criminal enterprise, and of conspiring to obstruct justice.

No executive was tried. Huawei and three subsidiaries, Huawei Device, Futurewei and Huawei Device USA, were the defendants. Judge Ann Donnelly set sentencing for September 14, 2027. Fines, forfeiture and restitution are not yet set, and Huawei says it will appeal.

## Iran, banks and borrowed ideas

Prosecutors said Huawei worked in Iran through a firm called Skycom, then told banks and US officials that Skycom was only a partner and that the company obeyed sanctions. The Justice Department says that was false, and that the lie protected access to dollar payments that global banks use. Officials also said Huawei helped Iranian authorities monitor and censor the internet.

On trade secrets, the government's evidence was sometimes less clever than a crime drama. It said engineers copied Cisco router code and left notes calling it "ocsic," Cisco backwards. A worker with a badge for "Weihua" was caught photographing Fujitsu equipment. Another, prosecutors said, carried part of T-Mobile's testing robot, Tappy, out of a lab in a backpack. The jury found a conspiracy to steal trade secrets. Those details are the government's account, not an itemized verdict. Huawei says the disputes were civil cases settled years ago, and that no court had ordered it to pay damages for stealing secrets.

## A split that both sides will quote

Racketeering law, often used against organized crime, asked whether crime was how Huawei was run. Jurors said no. Defense lawyer Brian Heberlig called that a profound rejection of the claim that the company was corrupt from top to bottom. Attorney General Todd Blanche said no person or company is above the law. Specific crimes were proved. A syndicate was not.

The prosecution followed the 2018 arrest in Canada of finance chief Meng Wanzhou. She later admitted misleading HSBC about Iran and returned to China under a deal. A 2019 US ban on Huawei gear, driven by spying fears, was not decided here. The FBI has linked the verdict to the Chinese state. That is the bureau's view, not a finding the jury made.

Huawei said the other charges lack legal or factual merit, and that clearing racketeering supports the stand it has taken for eight years. On Wednesday, foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said Beijing firmly opposes the United States suppressing and containing Chinese companies. He did not discuss the evidence. News reports say penalties could reach into the billions. Huawei's lawyer says the firm can pay. It already operates in more than 170 countries and is largely barred from US phone networks. Appeals will decide how much of Tuesday's split decision survives.
